blocks.text: Welcome to Japanese
Japanese uses three writing systems. Hiragana writes native words and grammar endings. Katakana writes many borrowed words and names. Kanji are characters that carry meaning.

blocks.title: A note about romaji
blocks.text: Romaji (Japanese written with Latin letters) can help at first. We will use less of it as you learn kana, so you can read Japanese directly.

blocks.title: How learning works
points: The curriculum chooses what comes next.

exercises.prompt: Which script commonly writes borrowed words?

feedback.explanation: Katakana commonly writes borrowed words and names.
こんにちは is a Japanese greeting meaning hello.

exercises.prompt: What helps you remember over time?

feedback.explanation: Reviews help strengthen memory over time.

blocks.text: Hiragana: A row
These five vowels are the basic sounds used throughout Japanese. Say each sound clearly and briefly.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: K row
Add k before each vowel sound: ka, ki, ku, ke, ko. Keep the vowel sounds the same as the first lesson.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: S row
Most sounds add s before the vowel. し is the irregular member: it is shi, not si.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: T row
Most sounds add t before the vowel. The irregular sounds are ち (chi) and つ (tsu).

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: N row
Add n before each vowel to make na, ni, nu, ne, no.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: H row
Most sounds add h before the vowel. ふ is conventionally romanized fu; its sound uses light friction between the lips, not a strong English f.

blocks.title: A common particle
blocks.text: When は marks the topic of a sentence, it is pronounced wa. The kana remains は.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: M row
Add m before each vowel: ma, mi, mu, me, mo.

blocks.title: Similar shapes
blocks.text: Compare む and す: む has a looped tail, while す crosses its loop.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: Y row
The y row has three kana: ya, yu, yo. There is no yi or ye in the basic Hiragana set.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: R row
The Japanese r is a brief tongue tap, unlike a strong English r or l.

blocks.title: Similar shapes
blocks.text: Compare る and ろ: ろ ends open; る curls back.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.
Hiragana: W row
The w row has わ and を, followed in the basic chart by ん. を is conventionally romanized wo, but as a particle in modern standard Japanese it is normally pronounced o.

blocks.title: Pronunciation
blocks.text: を remains the kana を and is normally pronounced o when used as the object particle in modern standard Japanese. ん is a moraic nasal, takes one beat, and changes articulation with its sound context; it is not always pronounced like an English n.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the hiragana alone.

Two small marks change consonant sounds: dakuten voices the k, s, t, and h rows; handakuten changes only the h row to p. ぢ and づ are usually read ji and zu in modern standard Japanese. They are uncommon outside established spellings and sound changes; じ and ず are much more common.

feedback.explanation: The small circle marks the h row with p sounds.
ぢ is normally read ji in modern standard Japanese.

blocks.text: A full-size kana ending in i combines with small ゃ, ゅ, or ょ. Read the pair as one blended mora: ki + small ya becomes kya. The second kana is small; a full-size や, ゆ, or よ is read separately.

feedback.explanation: Small ゃ blends with the kana before it.
Small ゅ blends with the kana before it.
Small ょ blends with the kana before it.

blocks.text: Small っ takes one beat and signals a brief stop before the next consonant. In romaji that consonant is often doubled: きって is kitte. Do not pronounce small っ as tsu.

feedback.explanation: Small っ adds a beat and doubles the following consonant.

blocks.text: Hiragana writes long vowels with kana, not the Katakana mark ー. おう and おお commonly make a long o sound; えい commonly makes a long e sound, while ええ also occurs. Learn each word spelling because patterns are not interchangeable in every word.

exercises.prompt: Which is a Hiragana long-vowel spelling?

feedback.explanation: おう is a common Hiragana spelling for a long o sound.

blocks.text: Katakana: A row
Start with the five steady vowel sounds. Katakana uses the same sounds as Hiragana, with a different shape, and commonly writes loanwords, many foreign names, and emphasis.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: K row
Add k before each vowel: ka, ki, ku, ke, ko.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: S row
Most sounds add s before the vowel. シ is irregular: read it shi, not si.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: T row
Most sounds add t before the vowel. チ is chi and ツ is tsu, not ti and tu.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: N row
Add n before each vowel to make na, ni, nu, ne, no.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: H row
Add h before each vowel. フ is conventionally romanized fu; its Japanese sound is made with the lips rather than a strong English f.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: M row
Add m before each vowel to make ma, mi, mu, me, mo.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: Y row
The y row has three base kana: ya, yu, and yo. There is no base yi or ye kana.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: R row
The Japanese r sound is a light tap, between English r and l.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Katakana: W row

The remaining base kana are ワ and the rare ヲ, followed by ン. ヲ is conventionally romanized wo, but in modern Japanese it is mainly the object particle and is pronounced like オ (o). ン is the standalone moraic n; its sound shifts slightly with the following consonant.

blocks.title: Read without romaji
blocks.text: Cover the readings above. Recall each sound from the katakana alone.
Dakuten and handakuten
Dakuten (゛) voices the k, s, t, and h rows. Handakuten (゜) changes the h row to p. Read each marked character as its own changed sound: シ is shi, ジ is ji, and ヂ is also commonly read ji.

feedback.explanation: The dakuten changes カ ka to ガ ga.
Handakuten changes ヒ hi to ピ pi.
The marked シ is read ji.

blocks.text: Small kana and contracted sounds

Small ャ, ュ, ョ combine with an eligible i-row sound: キ + ャ makes キャ kya. A small ッ marks a doubled consonant or brief stop before the next consonant, as in キット kitto. These readings depend on the neighboring kana.

feedback.explanation: キ and small ャ contract to kya.
シ and small ュ contract to shu.
リ and small ョ contract to ryo.
The next consonant is doubled or held with a brief stop.

blocks.text: Extended sounds and long vowels

Small vowels extend Katakana combinations for loanwords: ティ ti, ディ di, ファ fa, フィ fi, フェ fe, フォ fo, ウィ wi, ウェ we, ウォ wo, and チェ che. The long-vowel mark ー lengthens the preceding vowel: コーヒー is kōhī (coffee). Katakana uses ー for long vowels; do not apply Hiragana spelling rules.

feedback.explanation: テ and small ィ form ti.
フ and small ァ form fa.

exercises.prompt: What does ー do in コーヒー?

feedback.explanation: Each ー lengthens the vowel immediately before it.
チ and small ェ form che.

blocks.text: Introduce yourself

Use わたしは + a role or name + です。 to give a simple, polite introduction. は marks the topic and is pronounced wa here; です is the polite sentence ending. The pattern uses the topic and noun sentence forms you have already met.

blocks.title: Polite identity pattern
blocks.reading: わたしはがくせいです。

exercises.prompt: In わたしは学生です, which part marks the topic?

feedback.explanation: は follows わたし and marks the topic; here it is pronounced wa.

exercises.explanation: です completes this polite identity statement.

feedback.explanation: です completes this polite identity statement.

blocks.title: First meeting
blocks.text: はじめまして。 is a set polite expression used when meeting someone for the first time. It is often followed by an introduction.

exercises.explanation: Use topic, description, then です.

feedback.explanation: わたしは学生です。 is a polite way to say I am a student.
Names from outside Japan are commonly written in katakana.

blocks.title: Review
blocks.text: Vocabulary, phrase, and grammar cards from this lesson are added to spaced review.
People and family
You already know は for the topic and です for a polite noun sentence. Reuse that pattern to describe people in your family.

blocks.title: Whose family?
blocks.text: When speaking to someone outside your family, use 母 (はは) and 父 (ちち) for your own mother and father. Use お母さん (おかあさん) and お父さん (おとうさん) for another person’s parents or when addressing your own parents. The お…さん forms are respectful; they are not interchangeable in every context.

exercises.prompt: When telling someone about your own father, which term is usual?

feedback.explanation: 父 (ちち) is the usual term for your own father when speaking to someone outside your family.

exercises.explanation: Reuse です to finish the polite noun sentence.

feedback.explanation: 母は先生です。 says ‘My mother is a teacher.’
姉 is read あね and means my older sister.

exercises.prompt: Build ‘My older brother is a student.’
exercises.explanation: Use the familiar topic + description + です pattern.

feedback.explanation: 兄は学生です。 (あにはがくせいです。) means ‘My older brother is a student.’

blocks.text: Numbers and time
Build on the family lesson: use the numbers you learn here to say what time it is and how many people there are.

blocks.title: Some numbers have more than one reading
blocks.text: Four can be よん or し, seven can be なな or しち, and nine can be きゅう or く. Prefer よん, なな, and きゅう when counting by themselves. A counter can require another reading: 四時 is よじ, 七時 is しちじ, 九時 is くじ. Learn these useful combinations as whole forms.

blocks.title: Ask and tell the time
blocks.japanese: 今、何時ですか。四時半です。
blocks.reading: いま、なんじですか。よじはんです。
blocks.translation: What time is it now? It is half past four.

blocks.title: Minutes change sound
blocks.text: 分 is usually ふん or ぷん after a number. Remember these frequent clock readings: 一分 いっぷん, 三分 さんぷん, 四分 よんぷん, 六分 ろっぷん, 八分 はっぷん, 十分 じゅっぷん. The small っ holds the consonant briefly; ふ changes to ぷ in these forms.

exercises.prompt: Choose the reading of 四時.

feedback.explanation: 四時 uses the set clock reading よじ.

exercises.prompt: How do you say three minutes?

feedback.explanation: 三分 is さんぷん; the counter changes to ぷん.

blocks.title: Count people
blocks.reading: ひとり、ふたり、さんにん
blocks.translation: one person, two people, three people

blocks.title: One useful object counter
blocks.text: For a small number of general objects, つ is a useful starting point: 一つ (ひとつ), 二つ (ふたつ), 三つ (みっつ). This counter has its own readings. Japanese uses many other counters too; learn one when a real situation calls for it.

exercises.prompt: Write the common counting reading of 七.

feedback.explanation: 七 is often なな when counting; the clock form 七時 is しちじ.
二人 is the special form ふたり.

exercises.explanation: Put the time expression before the familiar polite ending です.

feedback.explanation: 四時半です。 means ‘It is half past four.’

blocks.text: Food and simple requests
Reuse the polite endings です and ですか from earlier lessons to talk about what you like and ask for food.

blocks.title: Say what you like
blocks.japanese: わたしは寿司が好きです。
blocks.reading: わたしはすしがすきです。

parts.meaning: as for me; は marks the topic (wa)
sushi; が marks the thing liked

blocks.title: Marking matters
blocks.text: 好き (すき, like) and 嫌い (きらい, dislike) commonly use が for the thing liked or disliked: 寿司が好きです. Do not copy English order and add を; が marks the liked thing. は can mark the overall topic: わたしは寿司が好きです. The speaker can be left unstated when it is clear.

blocks.reading: コーヒーがきらいです。

blocks.title: Ask for something politely
blocks.japanese: これをください。水をお願いします。
blocks.reading: これをください。みずをおねがいします。

parts.text: ください・お願いします
parts.reading: ください・おねがいします
parts.meaning: please give me; a courteous request

blocks.title: Polite requests
blocks.text: ください is a polite, practical request at a shop or restaurant. お願いします is another courteous option, as in 水をお願いします. Use すみません to get someone’s attention when appropriate.

exercises.prompt: Which particle marks sushi in the sentence 寿司___好きです。?

feedback.explanation: 好き commonly marks the liked thing with が.

exercises.explanation: を marks the requested item before ください.

feedback.explanation: これをください means ‘This, please.’

exercises.prompt: What does 水をお願いします mean?

feedback.explanation: 水 is water; お願いします makes a courteous request.
寿司 is read すし.

exercises.explanation: Put the item marked with を before お願いします.

feedback.explanation: 水をお願いします is a courteous request for water.

blocks.text: Places and location
You already know は for a topic, です for a polite statement, and か for a question. Reuse them to name a place and ask where something is.

blocks.title: This, that, and which?
blocks.japanese: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
blocks.reading: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
blocks.translation: this; that near you; that over there; which?

parts.meaning: that thing near the listener, or already mentioned
that thing away from both people
which thing? choose from known options

blocks.title: Things and places
blocks.text: これ・それ・あれ・どれ stand alone for things: これは何ですか。 asks “What is this?” To name a place, use ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ: ここは学校です means “This place is a school.” The こ set is near the speaker, そ near the listener, あ away from both, and ど asks a question. Use どれ for “which thing?” and どこ for “where?”

blocks.title: Name or ask about a place
blocks.japanese: ここは学校です。駅はどこですか。
blocks.reading: ここはがっこうです。えきはどこですか。
blocks.translation: This place is a school. Where is the station?

parts.meaning: marks the topic, as learned earlier

blocks.text: To say that something exists at a place, use [place] に [thing] が あります. に marks the place where it exists; が marks the thing that exists. Use あります for things and います for people and animals. These are polite present forms; います is not the same as the copula です.

blocks.title: Say what is at a place
blocks.japanese: うちにねこがいます。学校に店があります。
blocks.reading: うちにねこがいます。がっこうにみせがあります。
blocks.translation: There is a cat at home. There is a shop at the school.

parts.meaning: at home; at school (に marks the place)
a cat; a shop (が marks what exists)
exists: use います for a cat/person, あります for a thing/place

exercises.prompt: Which word means “that thing near the listener”?

feedback.explanation: それ points to a thing near the listener, or one already mentioned.

exercises.prompt: You and the listener are away from a place. Which word points there?

feedback.explanation: あそこ is a place away from both speaker and listener.

exercises.prompt: Complete “There is a cat at home.”
exercises.explanation: Use います for a living thing such as a cat.

feedback.explanation: ねこ is an animal, so use います.

exercises.prompt: Complete “There is a shop at the school.”
exercises.explanation: に marks the place where the shop exists.

feedback.explanation: に marks the place where something exists.
どこ asks which place or where.
どれ asks which thing from a known set.

exercises.explanation: Use the familiar topic + どこ + polite question pattern.

feedback.explanation: 駅はどこですか。 asks where the station is.

blocks.text: Everyday verbs and adjectives
Learn a few useful words for a normal day. Japanese often leaves out “I” when the person is clear; use わたしは when you want to name the topic.

Use the polite ます form for everyday statements. For a simple past statement, change ます to ました: 行きます → 行きました (go → went), 食べます → 食べました (eat → ate). The same pattern works for 勉強します → 勉強しました. You do not need to learn verb groups or casual forms yet.

blocks.title: Describe how something is
blocks.japanese: おいしいです。おいしかったです。
blocks.reading: おいしいです。おいしかったです。
blocks.translation: It is tasty. It was tasty.

parts.meaning: was tasty: change final い to かった

blocks.title: Present and past
blocks.text: ます and い-adjective + です describe now or a general fact. ました and い-adjective + かったです describe the past. This lesson practices positive statements only.

blocks.title: A simple routine
blocks.japanese: わたしは朝ごはんを食べます。学校へ行きます。
blocks.reading: わたしはあさごはんをたべます。がっこうへいきます。
blocks.translation: I eat breakfast. I go to school.

exercises.prompt: What does 食べました mean?

feedback.explanation: 食べます means “eat”; 食べました is its polite past form, “ate.”

exercises.explanation: Change the polite present ending ます to ました for this simple past form.

feedback.explanation: 勉強します → 勉強しました means “study” → “studied.”

exercises.explanation: For this i-adjective past pattern, replace its final い with かった.

feedback.explanation: おいしいです → おいしかったです.

exercises.prompt: Write “I go to school.” in Japanese.

feedback.explanation: 学校へ行きます。 means “I go to school”; the subject can be understood from context.

exercises.explanation: Put the item marked with を before the polite verb.

feedback.explanation: 水を飲みます。 means “I drink water.”

chunks.meaning: at home (で marks where an action happens)

exercises.explanation: Place the action location before the verb; ました marks past time.

feedback.explanation: うちで勉強しました。 means “I studied at home.”
